blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Is Mostly Water
blocks.text: A watermelon does not grow on a tree. It grows on a long vine that creeps along the ground. First a yellow flower opens. A bee lands on it and carries pollen from flower to flower. Then a tiny green ball starts to swell behind the flower. All summer it drinks and grows. It gets bigger than your head. Inside, the fruit is almost all water. If you filled ten cups with watermelon, more than nine of those cups would be water. That is why a cold slice tastes so good on a hot day. Even the green rind can be eaten. Some people pickle it.

blocks.prompt: From Desert Water Jug to Picnic Fruit
blocks.text: Almost every fruit you eat began as a wild plant somewhere. The watermelon began in Africa. Its wild cousins still grow in dry parts of that continent, where rain may not fall for months. Those wild melons are not sweet. Some are pale, some are bitter, and most are hard. But they hold water inside, and in a dry place water is worth more than sugar. Animals chew them open for a drink. People once carried them along on long walks across dry land. Farmers slowly changed the melon. Every year they saved seeds from the sweetest, reddest fruit and planted those seeds the next spring. Seed by seed, year by year, the melon got sweeter and softer and redder. It took thousands of years. The watermelon on your picnic table is the result: a desert plant that learned to taste like candy. Scientists have found watermelon seeds in Egyptian tombs. Some of those seeds are more than three thousand years old. Someone put them there on purpose, packed beside the dead for a long journey.

blocks.prompt: How to Read a Watermelon
blocks.text: A watermelon vine does something clever with its flowers. It makes two kinds. Male flowers open first and offer nothing but pollen. Female flowers come later, and behind each one sits a tiny green marble, the beginning of a fruit. That marble will only swell into a melon if a bee carries pollen from a male flower to it. Miss the delivery, and the marble shrivels and drops off the vine. Farmers know this, so they park beehives at the edge of the field. What happens next is mostly plumbing. The vine pulls water up out of the soil and pumps it into the fruit, day after day, through the whole hot summer. A ripe watermelon is about ninety two percent water by weight. Lift one and you are lifting a bag of rainwater the plant collected for you. The red color is not there for you either. It comes from lycopene, the same pigment that turns tomatoes red. To a wild animal, red says ripe, and ripe says eat me. The animal eats, walks away, and drops the seeds somewhere new. The plant cannot move, so it pays a passing animal in sugar to move for it. You can tell a ripe one without cutting it. Look for the pale patch where the melon sat on the dirt. On a ripe fruit that patch turns creamy yellow, not white. Thump it, and listen for a deep sound instead of a high one.

blocks.prompt: The Fruit People Argued Into Existence
blocks.text: Every watermelon is an argument that people won slowly. Start with the wild plant. The watermelon genus, Citrullus, is African. Its wild relatives sprawl across dry country, and most of them are nothing you would want to eat. The flesh is pale, firm, and often bitter with chemicals called cucurbitacins, which protect the plant from being chewed to pieces. What the wild melon does have is water, sealed in a tough rind that keeps it drinkable long after the rain has gone. In a dry season, a field of bitter melons is a reservoir. For a long time, botanists assumed the sweet watermelon descended from one of those bitter desert melons. In 2021 a team compared genomes and pointed somewhere else: the Kordofan melon of Sudan, a pale-fleshed, non-bitter melon that turns out to be the closest living relative of the fruit we grow. The bitter gourd of the Kalahari was a cousin, not a parent. Then came thousands of years of choosing. Farmers who saved seed from the least bitter, sweetest, reddest melons were doing genetics without knowing the word. Redness arrived because of a broken step. Plants normally convert lycopene, a red pigment, into other compounds. In the melon that conversion stalled, lycopene piled up, and the flesh went red. Sweetness and redness traveled together, and the fruit changed from a canteen into a dessert. Egyptian tomb paintings from about four thousand years ago show an oblong striped melon sliced on a tray, which is how you serve something sweet. Seeds and leaves have been found in tombs, including Tutankhamun's. The most recent trick is the seedless melon, and it is stranger than it looks. Breeders treat a normal plant so its cells carry four sets of chromosomes instead of two, then cross it with an ordinary two-set plant. The seed that results has three sets. Three does not divide evenly, so the plant cannot finish making seeds. The white flecks in a seedless slice are empty seed coats that never hardened. Here is the catch. A seedless plant still needs pollen, so growers must plant ordinary seeded melons in the same field and let the bees do the carrying.

blocks.prompt: Ninety Two Percent Water, and None of It an Accident
blocks.text: Cut a watermelon open and you are looking at a machine, though it takes some effort to see it that way. Start with the problem the plant is solving. Citrullus, the watermelon genus, is African, and its wild relatives grow where water arrives rarely and leaves fast. A plant rooted in that kind of country cannot go find a drink, and it cannot walk its children to better ground. It solves both problems with one object. It builds a thick rind around a reservoir of water, and it sells that reservoir to any animal willing to carry the seeds away. The rind is packaging. The water is payment. The seeds are the point. Most wild melons make the payment barely worth taking. Their flesh is pale and firm, and many are loaded with cucurbitacins, bitter compounds that discourage anything from eating too much. Bitterness is a defense, and for a wild plant it is a reasonable trade: lose a few customers, keep the fruit from being destroyed before the seeds are ready. People spent several thousand years arguing with that trade. Farmers saved seed from the least bitter fruit, then the sweetest, then the reddest, and each generation drifted a little further from the desert plant. For a long time botanists assumed the ancestor was one of the bitter Kalahari melons. A 2021 genome comparison pointed elsewhere, to the Kordofan melon of Sudan, a pale-fleshed, non-bitter melon that is the closest living relative of the fruit we grow. The domesticated watermelon did not tame a bitter gourd. It descended from something that was already halfway edible. The red is a mistake that people kept. Plants build carotenoid pigments in a chain, converting one into the next. In the watermelon, one step in that chain broke, so lycopene, the pigment that also makes tomatoes red, accumulated instead of being converted. That accident happened to travel alongside sweetness, and farmers, selecting for taste, kept dragging the red along with it. Egyptian tomb paintings from roughly four thousand years ago already show an oblong striped melon sliced on a tray, and you do not slice a bitter canteen and serve it on a tray. The strangest modern watermelon is the one with no seeds, which is a plant with a broken counting system. Breeders double a plant's chromosomes to four sets, cross it with an ordinary two-set plant, and get a seed carrying three. Three sets cannot be divided evenly in half, so seed formation stalls and the fruit fills with soft white flecks: seed coats that never hardened around anything. The joke is that a seedless watermelon is not self-sufficient. It still needs pollen to trigger the fruit, so growers plant ordinary seeded melons among them, and the bees do the rest. A fruit sold on the promise that it has no seeds cannot exist without a field of melons that do. Something was traded away in all of this. The sweet watermelon is a thirsty, sprawling crop that wants a long hot summer and a great deal of water. Its bitter cousins survive droughts that would kill it, and researchers now go back to those wild melons looking for the drought and disease genes that domestication left behind. The fruit that carries water everywhere is remarkably bad at getting water for itself. So the watermelon on the table is not a natural object. It is a four thousand year old collaboration between a desert vine that wanted its seeds moved and a species that wanted something sweet, and both sides got what they were after. The vine now grows on every continent except Antarctica. In the seedless fields, though, it has traded away the one thing it built the fruit for, and it cannot move its seeds anywhere without us.
